intro: Daniela wants a longer recess. Theo wants you to feel the snow fort fall in. Priya wants you to understand the Great Chicago Fire. Three writers, three jobs: an opinion, a story, an explanation. All three start with the same problem. The idea is clear in the writer's head and messy on the page.

This unit is about closing that gap. You will learn to build an opinion paragraph from a claim, reasons, examples and a closing. You will learn to zoom in on one small moment and make a reader see it, and to organize true facts so a reader can learn from them. Then you will learn what real writers know: the first draft is only the start, and revising, editing and reading aloud are where the writing gets good.
By the end, you will be able to plan a piece, draft it, make it stronger, make it correct, and hand it to a real reader, whether that reader is a friend, a class or the principal.
bigQuestion: How does a writer turn an idea in their head into words a reader can trust?

timeline.t: Pick the job: an opinion to argue, a moment to tell, or a topic to explain.
Map it in short phrases: claim and reasons, or the moment's beats, or groups of facts.
Write the whole thing fast and rough. Its only job is to exist.
Read the entire draft once without a pencil and ask what it needs next.
Add what is missing, cut what is extra, move what is misplaced, replace what is vague.
Give it to a peer. Hear one thing that worked and one honest question.
Swap weak verbs and vague nouns for strong, exact ones; vary sentence length.
One rule per pass: capitals, commas in a series, quotation marks, apostrophes, spelling.
Read it out loud with a finger on the words. Mark every stumble, then fix it.
Type a clean copy with a title, your name and the date. Keep the old drafts.
Give it to a real reader. A message is not finished until someone receives it.

words.d: an opinion you state and are ready to defend with reasons
an answer to why that supports a claim
a specific fact, number or moment that shows a reason is true
a word that connects ideas, such as because, for example, also or therefore
the person or people who will read your writing
one short event a true story zooms in on
a detail that uses sight, sound, touch, smell or taste
words or details from a text that prove a point about it
a word or phrase that moves the reader from one part or idea to the next
to change what a piece says: its ideas, order and details
to fix capitals, punctuation, spelling and grammar
what a reader tells a writer about how the writing worked

choices: The library should stay open after school.
test.why: A claim takes a side someone could argue against. The others are plain facts.

test.q: Daniela's reader was the principal. Which reason would that reader care about most?
choices: Kids who move learn faster afterward.
test.why: A strong reason matters to the reader. Principals care about learning.

test.q: Which is the most specific example?
choices: The math page took twenty-five minutes on Wednesday.
test.why: Specific means exact: a day and a number.

test.q: Which linking word introduces a result or closing?
test.why: Therefore means for that reason and leads into a closing.

test.q: What does naming the other side do for an opinion?
choices: Makes it stronger by answering what the reader already wonders
test.why: Readers think of objections on their own. Answering first shows careful thinking.

test.q: What makes a letter different from a paragraph in a notebook?
choices: It has a real audience, a greeting and a request
test.why: A letter goes to a real person and asks for something.

test.q: Theo's first draft covered his whole snow day in six sentences. What was the problem?
choices: It was a list, not a story
test.why: A whole day in six sentences cannot slow down. A story zooms in on one moment.

test.q: Which sentence uses a sensory detail?
choices: The cold crept inside my gloves and my fingers went stiff.
test.why: Touch details let the reader feel the cold instead of being told about it.

test.q: What is the second job of informative writing, after naming the topic?
test.why: Grouping turns loose facts into paragraphs a reader can follow.

test.q: In a how-to, what should each step start with?
test.why: Steps are commands: fold, cut, spread.

test.q: You write about a text. After the point and the evidence, what comes next?
choices: An explanation of how the evidence proves the point

test.q: Which is a revising move, not an editing fix?
test.why: Revising changes what the piece says. Cutting is one of the four revising moves.

test.q: Which feedback helps a writer most?
choices: I lost track of the time. How long did you look?
test.why: Specific feedback with an honest question gives the writer something to fix.
The question mark goes inside the closing quotation mark, and the tag follows in lowercase.

test.q: Why does reading your draft aloud help?
choices: Your ears catch what your eyes skip
It is faster than reading silently
test.why: Your eyes read what you meant; your ears hear what is really on the page.

write.prompt: Mr. Nguyen said, "Good writing is mostly rewriting." Do you agree? Write an opinion paragraph that makes a claim, gives two reasons with examples from this unit, and answers the other side.
tips: Claim: take a clear side in one sentence. Do not say kind of or maybe.
Evidence: use what happened to Theo's snow-day drafts, Mr. Nguyen's four drafts on the wall, or Daniela's two versions.
Reasoning: explain how each example proves your reason. Point, evidence, explain.
The other side: some writers say a first draft is enough if it is true. Name that view fairly and answer it.
Close by restating your claim in new words, then read the whole paragraph aloud before you hand it in.

title: Writing

chapters.title: The Paragraph: a Claim and Reasons
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you make a reader believe what you think?

story.title: Twenty Minutes Is Not Enough
story.kicker: A fourth grader thinks recess should be longer. Thinking it is easy. Proving it takes work.
paragraphs: Daniela's school in Chicago gives fourth graders twenty minutes of recess. By the time the class walks outside, ten minutes are gone. She wants recess to be longer. On Monday her teacher, Mr. Beck, says the class will write opinions about a school question. Daniela knows her question right away.

Her first draft is one sentence: "Recess should be longer because it is fun." Mr. Beck reads it and asks, "Would the principal change the schedule because it is fun?" Daniela thinks about it. No. Fun is true, but it is not a reason a principal would care about.

So she looks for better reasons. She asks the gym teacher, who says kids need at least sixty minutes of movement a day. She counts how many minutes the class really gets outside: ten. She notices that after recess, the room is quieter and math goes faster. Now she has three reasons, and each one has a fact behind it.

Her second draft has a topic sentence, three reasons, an example for each and a closing line. She even adds a sentence about the other side: "Some people say longer recess means less learning time. But a calm class learns more in forty minutes than a wiggly class learns in fifty."

Mr. Beck reads it twice. "Now this is an argument," he says. "Who should read it?" Daniela smiles. "The principal." She writes it again as a letter, and on Friday she puts it in the office mailbox herself.
story.think: Why was "because it is fun" a weak reason? What made Daniela's new reasons stronger?

lessons.title: The Topic Sentence Takes a Side
lessons.mainIdea: A topic sentence tells your reader exactly what you believe in one clear sentence.
reading: Read these two sentences. "Recess is a part of the school day." "Recess should be twenty minutes longer." The first one is just true. Nobody would argue with it. The second one takes a side. Someone could disagree. That second sentence is a *claim*. A claim is an opinion you are ready to defend.

In an opinion paragraph, the claim goes first. It is the *topic sentence*, the sentence that tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about. A good topic sentence is short, clear and bold. It does not say "I kind of think maybe." It says "Our school should start a garden."

Try this test on your own topic sentence. Could someone argue against it? If yes, it is a claim. If no, it is only a fact. "Dogs are animals" is a fact. "Dogs make better pets than cats" is a claim. Facts belong later, as proof. The claim comes first.

words.d: an opinion you state and are ready to defend with reasons
the sentence that tells what a whole paragraph is about
what a person thinks or believes; other people can disagree with it

look.title: Fact or Claim?
look.text: Look at these four sentences. 1. Our library is open on Tuesdays. 2. Our library should be open on Saturdays too. 3. Third graders should get to pick their own seats. 4. Third graders sit in rows.
look.prompt: Which two sentences are claims? How can you tell?

check.q: What makes a sentence a claim?
choices: It has a number in it
check.why: A claim takes a side. If someone could argue against it, it is a claim, not just a fact.

check.q: Where does the claim go in an opinion paragraph?
choices: In the topic sentence, at the start
check.why: The claim is the topic sentence. It comes first so the reader knows what the paragraph is about.

check.q: Which sentence is a claim?
choices: Our school should serve lunch later.
The gym has a basketball hoop.
check.why: "Our school should serve lunch later" takes a side. The others are facts nobody would argue about.

lessons.title: Reasons Hold the Claim Up
lessons.mainIdea: A reason answers the question why, and a strong reason is one your reader would care about.
reading: A claim by itself is like a table top with no legs. It falls over. "Recess should be longer." Why? The answers to why are the *reasons*, and they are the legs. Daniela's first reason was "because it is fun." That is a real reason, but it is weak. A principal does not plan the day around fun.

A strong reason is one your reader would care about. Daniela's reader was the principal. Principals care about learning, health and safety. So her strong reasons were: kids need sixty minutes of movement a day, the class only gets ten minutes outside, and a class that has moved learns faster. Each reason is something the principal already wants.

Aim for two or three reasons. One reason is thin. Six reasons make a list, not a paragraph. Pick the strongest and put them in order. Many writers save the best reason for last, so it is the one the reader remembers.

words.d: an answer to why that supports a claim
to hold something up; reasons support a claim

look.title: Pick the Reader's Reason
look.text: Marcus wants the class to read outside on warm days. He lists reasons: 1. It is nice out. 2. Fresh air helps kids stay awake and focused. 3. He likes the sun. 4. The class would get quieter because there is more room to spread out. His reader is his teacher.
look.prompt: Which two reasons would his teacher care about most? Why?

check.q: What question does a reason answer?
check.why: A reason answers why the claim is true. The claim says what; the reasons say why.

check.q: Why was "because it is fun" a weak reason for the principal?
choices: The principal does not plan the day around fun
check.why: A strong reason is one the reader cares about. Principals care about learning and health more than fun.

check.q: How many reasons does a good opinion paragraph usually have?
check.why: One reason is thin, and six or more become a list. Two or three strong reasons work best.

lessons.title: Examples Make Reasons Real
lessons.mainIdea: An example is a specific fact or moment that shows a reason is true.
reading: Here is a reason: "Our class learns better after recess." It sounds good, but a reader might shrug. Now add this: "Last Tuesday, after twenty minutes outside, we finished the math page in ten minutes. On Wednesday, with no recess, it took twenty-five." Now the reader can see it. That is an *example*.

An example is a specific fact, number, story or moment. Specific means exact: not "a lot of kids" but "eighteen of twenty-four kids." Not "one time" but "last Tuesday." Examples come from things you saw, counted, read or asked someone about. Daniela asked the gym teacher and counted minutes with a clock.
Each reason should get at least one example. Write the reason, then write the example right after it. The reason is the rule; the example is the proof. Together they make a pair the reader can trust.

words.d: a specific fact, number or moment that shows a reason is true
exact and detailed, not vague

look.title: Minutes to Finish the Math Page
look.cite: Daniela's class log, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which day stands out? How could Daniela use these numbers as an example?

check.q: What is an example in an opinion paragraph?
choices: A specific fact or moment that proves a reason
check.why: An example is specific proof. It shows the reader that the reason is true.

check.q: Which of these is the most specific?
check.why: Specific means exact. A real count is stronger than words like some, lots or everybody.

check.q: Where does an example go?
choices: Right after the reason it proves
check.why: The example belongs right after its reason, so the two read as a pair: the rule, then the proof.

lessons.title: Linking Words Connect Ideas
lessons.mainIdea: Linking words like because, for example, also and therefore show the reader how your sentences fit together.
reading: Read this. "Recess should be longer. Kids need to move. The class only gets ten minutes outside." The ideas are there, but the sentences sit like bricks with no mortar. Now read it again. "Recess should be longer because kids need to move. For example, our class only gets ten minutes outside." The words because and for example are the mortar.

These are *linking words*. Each one tells the reader what kind of idea is coming. Because and since introduce a reason. For example and for instance introduce an example. Also, another and in addition add one more reason. Therefore, so and that is why introduce a result or a closing.

Use linking words on purpose, not everywhere. One per new idea is enough. If every sentence starts with also, the paragraph sounds like a list. Mix them, and your reader can follow the path from claim to reasons to closing without getting lost.

words.d: a word or phrase that connects one idea to the next, such as because or also
a linking word that means for that reason; it introduces a result

look.title: One Paragraph, Linked
look.text: Our class should keep a pet fish because caring for an animal teaches responsibility. For example, someone must feed it every single day, even on Fridays. Also, watching a fish calms people down. Therefore, a fish would help us learn and help us focus.
look.cite: Model paragraph, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the four linking words. What job does each one do?

check.q: Which linking word introduces a reason?
check.why: Because tells the reader that a reason is coming. For example introduces an example, also adds, and therefore closes.

check.q: Which linking word means for that reason?
check.why: Therefore introduces a result or closing. It means for that reason.

check.q: What happens if every sentence starts with also?
choices: The reader gets confused about the topic
The paragraph sounds like a list
check.why: Linking words should be mixed and used on purpose. Too many of the same one sounds like a list.

lessons.title: The Closing Sentence
lessons.mainIdea: A closing sentence restates the claim in new words and leaves the reader with something to remember.
reading: A paragraph without a closing sentence feels like a song that stops in the middle. The reader waits for more. The *closing sentence* is the last sentence, and it does two jobs. First, it says the claim again in new words. Second, it leaves the reader with a feeling or a thought to carry away.

Daniela's claim was "Recess should be twenty minutes longer." Her closing sentence was "Give us those twenty minutes, and you will get a calmer, healthier, smarter fourth grade." Same idea, new words, and a picture of what the reader gains. Notice that she did not just copy her topic sentence.

Two ways to close. You can *restate* the claim with a linking word: "That is why our school needs a garden." Or you can call the reader to act: "Plant the garden this spring." Do not add a brand new reason at the end. New reasons belong in the middle; the end is for landing.

words.d: the last sentence of a paragraph; it restates the claim and finishes the idea
to say the same idea again in different words

look.title: Three Endings
look.text: The claim is "Our class should visit the Field Museum." Here are three possible closings. A. Also, the museum has a gift shop. B. That is why the Field Museum is the right trip for us. C. Our class should visit the Field Museum.
look.prompt: Which closing works best? What is wrong with each of the other two?

check.q: What does a closing sentence do?
choices: Restates the claim in new words
check.why: The closing says the claim again in new words and leaves the reader with something to remember.

check.q: Why should you not copy the topic sentence word for word at the end?
choices: The reader has already read it; new words land better
The paragraph would get too long
check.why: Restating means new words for the same idea. An exact copy feels flat.

check.q: Which is a call to act?
choices: A garden is a place where plants grow.
check.why: A call to act tells the reader to do something. Plant the garden is a command.

lessons.title: Plan Before You Draft
lessons.mainIdea: A short plan, made before you write, keeps your paragraph in order and saves you from starting over.
reading: Picture a builder who starts nailing boards before drawing a plan. The house comes out crooked. Writers who start drafting with no plan get crooked paragraphs: a reason with no example, or a closing that forgets the claim. So before you draft, make a *plan*. It takes five minutes and saves twenty.

A plan for an opinion paragraph can be a simple box chart. Top box: the claim. Under it, two or three boxes, one per reason. Under each reason, a line for its example. Bottom box: the closing. Daniela filled hers in with short phrases, not full sentences: "60 min movement, gym teacher said."

When the plan is full, look at it before you write. Is any reason weak? Cut it. Does a reason have no example? Find one or cut it. Is the best reason last? Move it. Fixing the plan is easy. Fixing a finished paragraph is hard. Then *draft*: turn each box into one or two full sentences.

words.d: a short map of what you will write, made before drafting
to write a first full version of a piece

look.title: A Plan With a Hole
look.text: Look at Jamal's plan. Claim: Fourth graders should have a class job chart. Reason 1: everyone knows what to do. Example: last year we fought over who feeds the fish. Reason 2: it is fair. Example: (blank). Closing: A job chart makes the room run smoothly.
look.prompt: What is missing from the plan? What could Jamal do about it before he drafts?

check.q: When should you make a plan?
check.why: The plan comes first. It is much easier to fix a plan than a finished paragraph.

check.q: What goes in the plan?
choices: The claim, reasons, examples and closing, in short phrases
check.why: A plan maps every part of the paragraph in short phrases, not full sentences.

check.q: Your plan shows a reason with no example. What is the best move?
choices: Find an example or cut the reason
Make the reason the topic sentence
Add three more reasons with no examples
check.why: Every reason needs an example. Fix the hole in the plan before you draft.

lessons.title: Your Opinion About a Book
lessons.mainIdea: When you write an opinion about a book, your reasons come from what actually happens in the book.
reading: "This book was good" is not a claim anyone can use. Good how? For whom? A real book opinion sounds like this: "Third graders who like animals should read this book." Or: "The ending of this book is not fair to the main character." Now there is something to argue.

For a book opinion, your examples come from inside the book. A reason might be "The main character is brave." The example is a moment: "When the barn catches fire, she runs back in for the calf." Point to a page or a scene. Readers trust you more when you show that you really read it.

You can also give the *reader* of your opinion a job. Say who should read the book and why. Say whether you would read it again. Say what you wished the author had done. Those are all claims. Back each one with a scene, and you have a book *review* a friend could actually use.

words.d: a piece of writing that gives an opinion about a book, movie or game, with reasons
the person who will read what you write; you write with that person in mind

look.title: A Book Opinion, Short
look.text: Kids who like scary stories should read The Lighthouse Key. The main reason is that the author makes you wait. For example, in chapter four the door creaks for a whole page before anyone opens it. Also, the ending answers every question but one, which makes you want a second book. Read it with the lights on.
look.cite: Model review of an imaginary book, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What is the claim? What example from inside the book supports the first reason?

check.q: Why is "This book was good" a weak claim?
choices: It does not say good how, or for whom
check.why: A useful book claim says something a reader can argue with, like who should read it or whether the ending is fair.

check.q: Where do the examples for a book opinion come from?
check.why: Examples come from inside the book: a scene, a chapter, a page. That shows you really read it.

check.q: Which is a claim a book review could make?
choices: The book came out in March.
The ending is not fair to the main character.
check.why: The other three are facts. The ending being unfair is an opinion someone could argue with.

lessons.title: Considering the Other Side
lessons.mainIdea: Naming what the other side thinks, and answering it, makes your opinion stronger, not weaker.
reading: Daniela wrote: "Some people say longer recess means less learning time. But a calm class learns more in forty minutes than a wiggly class learns in fifty." She named the *other side*, the opinion that disagrees with hers. Then she answered it. This is one of the strongest moves an opinion writer can make.

Why does it help? Because your reader is already thinking of the other side. The principal was going to think "but learning time" the moment she read the claim. If Daniela says it first, the principal sees that Daniela thought hard. If Daniela hides it, the principal thinks Daniela never noticed.

The shape is simple. "Some people think ____. But ____." Give the other side a fair sentence, not a silly one. Then answer it with a reason or an example. Put it near the end, just before your closing. One other-side sentence and one answer is enough for a paragraph.

words.d: the opinion of people who disagree with your claim
to reply to the other side with a reason or example that shows why your claim still stands

look.title: Fair or Silly?
look.text: Two writers argue that the class should get to choose its own books. Writer A says: "Some people think kids would pick baby books. But last month every kid in our class chose a chapter book from the free bin." Writer B says: "Some people think choosing books is dumb, but they are wrong."
look.prompt: Which writer gives the other side a fair sentence and a real answer? What is missing from the other one?

check.q: What is the other side?
choices: The opinion of people who disagree with your claim
check.why: The other side is what people who disagree would say. Naming it shows you thought hard.

check.q: Why does naming the other side make your opinion stronger?
choices: The reader was already thinking it, and you answer it first
It replaces the need for examples
It lets you skip the closing
check.why: Readers think of objections on their own. Answering first shows you have considered them.

check.q: Where does the other side usually go in a paragraph?
choices: Near the end, before the closing
check.why: Name and answer the other side just before the closing, so the paragraph ends on your claim.

lessons.title: A Letter to the Principal
lessons.mainIdea: A letter turns your opinion paragraph into a message for a real person, with a greeting, a polite tone and a request.
reading: An opinion paragraph in a notebook changes nothing. The same paragraph in a letter to the principal might change the schedule. A letter has a real *audience*, the person who will read it. When you know your audience, you choose your reasons, your words and your tone for that one person.

A friendly letter has parts. The date at the top. A greeting: "Dear Dr. Alvarez,". The body, which is your opinion paragraph. A closing word like "Sincerely," and your name. Daniela added one more thing at the end of the body: a clear request. "Please consider adding twenty minutes to fourth-grade recess this spring."

Tone matters. Tone is how your words sound to the reader. "Recess is way too short and it is not fair" sounds like complaining. "Our class would learn more with twenty more minutes outside" sounds like a person with a plan. Polite and specific beats loud every time. Then proofread it, sign it and send it.

words.d: the person or people who will read your writing
how your words sound to the reader, such as polite, angry or excited
a polite ask for something specific

look.title: The Ending of Daniela's Letter
look.text: Some people say longer recess means less learning time. But a calm class learns more in forty minutes than a wiggly class learns in fifty. Please consider adding twenty minutes to fourth-grade recess this spring. Give us those twenty minutes, and you will get a calmer, healthier, smarter fourth grade. Sincerely, Daniela Ruiz
look.prompt: Find the other side, the request and the closing. What tone do the words have?

check.q: What is an audience?
choices: The closing word of a letter
The reason a claim is true
The person who will read your writing
check.why: The audience is your reader. Knowing your audience shapes your reasons and tone.

check.q: Which sounds like the better tone for a letter to the principal?
choices: Our class would learn more with twenty more minutes outside.
Recess is way too short and it is not fair!
check.why: Polite and specific works better than complaining. The first one sounds like a person with a plan.

check.q: What did Daniela add to the end of her letter's body?
check.why: A letter asks for something. Daniela ended with a specific, polite request.

review.q: Which of these is a claim, not a fact?
choices: The gym is next to the office.
review.why: A claim takes a side that someone could argue against. The others are facts.

review.q: What is the job of a reason?
choices: To say why the claim is true
review.why: Reasons answer why. They are the legs that hold the claim up.

review.q: Which sentence gives a specific example?
choices: On Wednesday, with no recess, the math page took twenty-five minutes.
review.why: An example is exact: a day, a number, a moment. The others are vague.

review.q: Which linking word introduces an example?
review.why: For instance and for example introduce examples. Because and since introduce reasons; therefore closes.

review.q: What should a closing sentence NOT do?
choices: Restate the claim in new words
Leave the reader with a thought
review.why: New reasons belong in the middle. The closing restates and lands the idea.

review.q: Why make a plan before drafting?
choices: It is easier to fix a plan than a finished paragraph
review.why: A plan shows holes, like a reason with no example, while they are still easy to fix.

review.q: Daniela wrote, "Some people say longer recess means less learning time. But a calm class learns more." What is she doing?
choices: Naming and answering the other side
review.why: She names the opposing opinion fairly, then answers it with a reason.

review.q: What changes when an opinion paragraph becomes a letter?
choices: It gets a real audience, a greeting and a request
It no longer needs a closing
review.why: A letter goes to a real person. It adds a greeting, a polite tone and a specific request.

chapters.title: Stories and Explanations
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you make a true thing come alive on the page, whether it is a moment or a fact?

story.title: The Snow Day, Twice
story.kicker: Theo writes about a snow day. The first draft is true. The second draft is true and alive.
paragraphs: In January a storm dropped eleven inches of snow on Chicago, and school closed. On Monday, Ms. Okafor asked her fourth graders to write a true story about the snow day. Theo wrote fast. "I woke up. It was a snow day. I played outside with my brother. It was fun. Then I came in and had hot chocolate. The end."

Ms. Okafor read it and said, "Every word of this is true. And I cannot see any of it." Theo looked at the page. She was right. It could have been anyone's snow day. "Pick one part," she said. "The smallest part that mattered. Then slow down and show me."

Theo picked the moment the snow fort fell in. He closed his eyes and remembered. The wall had been taller than his brother, Eli. Eli had pushed one more block onto the top. There had been a soft whump, and then Eli's boots sticking out of a white pile, and Eli's muffled voice: "I'm okay! I'm okay!"

His second draft started in the middle of the action. "Eli lifted the last block over his head. 'Don't,' I said. He did." He added the whump. He added the cold that got inside his gloves. He added what Eli's voice sounded like from under the snow. He ended with the two of them lying in the wreck of the fort, laughing so hard they could not stand up.
When Theo read it aloud, two kids laughed at the whump. Ms. Okafor taped both drafts to the wall side by side. "Same day," she said. "Same boy. One of these is a list. The other one is a story."
story.think: Theo's first draft was true. Why did his teacher say she could not see it? What did he change?

lessons.title: Pick One Small Moment
lessons.mainIdea: A strong true story zooms in on one small moment instead of listing a whole day.
reading: Theo's first draft covered a whole day in six sentences. Wake up, play, come in, drink cocoa. That is a list, and a list is not a story. A story needs a camera that stops and holds still. Ms. Okafor told him to find the smallest part that mattered. He found ten seconds: the fort falling in.

Writers call this a *small moment*. It is one event that took a few minutes, or even a few seconds. The bus pulling away without you. The moment your dog first saw snow. The second the cake fell over. Small moments make better stories because you can slow down and show every detail.

To find yours, start with a big memory. Then ask: what is the one part I would tell a friend first? That is the moment. Everything else is background. You can mention the rest in a sentence, but the moment gets the whole page.

words.d: one short event, a few seconds or minutes long, that a true story zooms in on
a story, true or made up, that tells events in order

look.title: Zoom In
look.text: Lena's big memory is her birthday. Inside it are smaller moments: blowing out the candles, opening a box that turned out to have a kitten in it, her grandma singing off key, the kitten hiding under the couch for an hour. Lena has to pick one.
look.prompt: Which small moment would you choose to write about? What could you show in it that a list would leave out?

check.q: Why was Theo's first draft a list instead of a story?
choices: It covered a whole day in six sentences with no details
check.why: A whole day in six sentences cannot slow down. A story needs to hold still on one moment.

check.q: What is a small moment?
choices: A story about a small person
The last sentence of a story
One short event you zoom in on
check.why: A small moment is one event that took a few minutes or seconds, told with detail.

check.q: How can you find your small moment inside a big memory?
choices: Ask what part you would tell a friend first
Write the whole day, then stop
check.why: The part you would tell first is the part that mattered. That is the moment to zoom in on.

lessons.title: A Beginning That Hooks
lessons.mainIdea: Start inside the action, with a line of talk, a sound or a picture, so the reader has to keep going.
reading: Compare two first lines. "I woke up. It was a snow day." And: "Eli lifted the last block over his head. 'Don't,' I said. He did." The first one could begin a thousand stories. The second one makes you ask what happens next. That pull is called a *hook*.

Three kinds of hooks work well for a small moment. Start with action: someone is already doing something. Start with talk: a line of *dialogue*, the words a person says. Start with a sound or a picture: "Whump. Then silence, then boots." Any of these drops the reader into the moment instead of walking them to it.

What does not work? Starting at the start of the day. Starting with "I am going to tell you about." Starting with the weather unless the weather is the story. Try this: write your moment, then cut the first two sentences. Often the real hook was hiding in sentence three.

words.d: an opening that grabs the reader and makes them want to keep reading
the words characters say, shown with quotation marks

look.title: Three Openings for One Moment
look.text: 1. It was a Saturday and I was at the pool with my cousin. 2. "Jump," my cousin said. "I'm counting to three." 3. The diving board bounced under my feet, and the water looked a mile away.
look.prompt: Which opening is the weakest hook? What do the other two do that it does not?

check.q: What is a hook?
choices: The last line of a story
An opening that makes the reader want to keep going
A line that explains the setting
check.why: A hook grabs the reader at the start. It makes them ask what happens next.

check.q: Which opening starts with dialogue?
choices: The board bounced under my feet.
check.why: Dialogue is the words a person says. "Jump," my cousin said, starts with talk.

check.q: What trick can help you find a better hook?
choices: Add a sentence about the weather
Start with "I am going to tell you about"
Cut the first two sentences and see what is left
check.why: The real hook is often in sentence three. Cutting the slow start reveals it.

lessons.title: Talk and the Five Senses
lessons.mainIdea: Dialogue and sensory details let the reader hear, see and feel the moment instead of being told about it.
reading: "It was fun" tells. "Eli's boots stuck out of the pile and his muffled voice said, 'I'm okay! I'm okay!'" shows. The difference is *detail*. Theo's second draft gave the reader things to hear, see and feel. Those are called *sensory details*: details that use the five senses of sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.

You do not need all five in every paragraph. Pick the two or three that were strongest in the moment. For the fort, it was sound (whump, muffled voice) and touch (cold inside the gloves). Ask yourself: what did I hear? What did my hands feel? What could I smell? Write the honest answer.

Dialogue is another way to show. When Eli says "I'm okay!" twice, we learn he is scared and also fine, and we learn it faster than if Theo explained it. Keep dialogue short and real. People do not give speeches in a snow fort. Two or three lines of talk in a small moment is usually plenty.

words.d: a detail that uses one of the five senses: sight, sound, touch, smell or taste
a small, specific piece of a picture, sound or feeling
letting the reader see and hear the moment instead of just naming the feeling

look.title: Sensory Details in Theo's Two Drafts
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the story drafts described above
look.prompt: What do the numbers say about the difference between a list and a story?

check.q: Which sentence uses a sensory detail?
choices: The cold got inside my gloves.
check.why: Cold inside the gloves is a touch detail. The others tell without showing.

check.q: How many senses should you use in one paragraph?
choices: The two or three that were strongest in the moment
check.why: Pick the senses that were really strong in that moment. Forcing all five sounds fake.

check.q: What does Eli's "I'm okay! I'm okay!" show the reader?
choices: That Eli is angry at Theo
That Eli is scared but fine
That the fort is still standing
check.why: Short real dialogue shows feeling fast. Saying it twice shows he is shaken but not hurt.

lessons.title: An Ending That Satisfies
lessons.mainIdea: A good ending lands on the feeling of the moment; it does not just stop or say the end.
reading: Theo's first draft ended with "The end." His second ended with the brothers lying in the wreck of the fort, laughing too hard to stand up. The first ending stops. The second one lands. It leaves the reader with the feeling the whole story was building toward.

Three ways to land a small moment. End with a picture: the last thing you saw. End with a line of talk: the last thing someone said. End with a thought: what you knew or felt right then, in one honest sentence. "We never rebuilt the fort. We did not need to." Any of these gives the story a place to rest.

What to avoid. Do not race to bedtime: "Then we went in and ate and went to sleep." Do not explain the lesson: "And that is why you should listen to your brother." Trust the reader. If you showed the moment well, they already feel it. Stop one sentence sooner than you think you should.

words.d: the last part of a story, where it lands on a feeling, picture or thought
feeling complete and right, so the reader does not need more

look.title: Which Landing?
look.text: A story about a lost dog found in the rain. Three endings. A. Then we went home and had dinner and went to bed. The end. B. She was soaked, and she smelled terrible, and I did not let go of her all the way home. C. The lesson is that you should always keep your dog on a leash.
look.prompt: Which ending lands on the feeling? What is wrong with the other two?

check.q: What is the difference between an ending that stops and one that lands?
choices: A landing ending leaves the reader with the story's feeling
A stopping ending has more dialogue
check.why: A landing gives the reader a place to rest on the feeling. Stopping just quits.

check.q: Which is an ending that races to bedtime?
choices: I did not let go of her all the way home.
Then we ate and went to sleep. The end.
The fort was gone, and I did not mind.
check.why: Racing to bedtime skips past the moment to finish the day. It drains the feeling out.

check.q: Why should you not explain the lesson at the end?
choices: Lessons are not allowed in stories
The teacher will take points off
It makes the story too short
If you showed the moment well, the reader already feels it
check.why: Trust the reader. A well-shown moment carries its own meaning.

lessons.title: Introduce and Group the Facts
lessons.mainIdea: Informative writing opens by naming the topic, then puts related facts together in groups.
reading: A story shows one moment. An *informative* piece explains a topic so a reader learns something true. Both are true writing, but they work differently. The story slows down. The informative piece organizes. Its first job is to tell the reader the topic in a sentence or two: "Monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles every fall, and Illinois is on their road."

The second job is *grouping*. Imagine you have twelve facts about monarchs on sticky notes. Some are about the wings. Some are about the trip south. Some are about milkweed. Put the wing facts together, the trip facts together, the food facts together. Each group becomes a paragraph. A reader can follow three groups; a reader cannot follow twelve loose facts.

Order the groups so they make sense. Often it is what a thing is, then what it does, then why it matters. The introduction names the topic and hints at the groups: "Monarchs have amazing wings, make an incredible trip, and need one plant to survive." Now the reader knows the map before the trip.

words.d: writing that explains a topic and gives true facts
what a piece of writing is about
to put facts that belong together into one paragraph

look.title: Sort the Sticky Notes
look.text: Six facts about the Chicago River: it once flowed into Lake Michigan; engineers reversed it in 1900; it is dyed green on St. Patrick's Day; it flows through downtown; boats give tours on it; reversing it kept waste out of the drinking water.
look.prompt: Which facts belong together? What would you name each group?

check.q: What is the first job of an informative piece?
choices: Start with a hook of dialogue
check.why: Informative writing names its topic first so the reader knows what they are learning.

check.q: Why group facts?
choices: A reader can follow a few groups but not many loose facts
Because facts must be in alphabetical order
check.why: Grouping turns a pile of facts into paragraphs a reader can follow.

check.q: How does an informative piece differ from a small-moment story?
choices: It organizes facts instead of slowing down on one moment
check.why: Both can be true. The story zooms in; the informative piece organizes what the reader needs to learn.

lessons.title: Headings, Pictures and Definitions
lessons.mainIdea: Headings, pictures and defined words help a reader find and understand the facts.
reading: Open a true book about volcanoes. You do not read every page. You look at the *headings*, the short bold titles above each part, and jump to the one you want. When you write informative text, give your reader the same help. Each group of facts gets a heading that says what it is about: "The Long Trip South."

A picture with a *caption* can carry a fact faster than a paragraph. A map with an arrow from Illinois to Mexico shows the monarch's trip in one look. A labeled drawing of a wing shows the scales. Draw it or find it, then write a caption: one sentence that tells what the picture shows.

Every topic has words the reader might not know. Milkweed. Migration. Do not skip them and do not just use them. *Define* them: give the meaning in plain words the first time the word appears. "Monarchs migrate, which means they travel a long way when the seasons change." A defined word is a gift to a reader who was about to get lost.

words.d: a short bold title above a part of a text that says what the part is about
one sentence under a picture that tells what it shows
to give the meaning of a word in plain words

look.title: One Section With Its Helpers
look.text: Heading: One Plant to Live On. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, a tall plant with thick leaves and a milky sap. Without milkweed, a monarch cannot grow up. Illinois has more than a dozen kinds of milkweed. Caption under a drawing: A monarch caterpillar, striped yellow, black and white, on a milkweed leaf.
look.cite: Model section written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the heading, the defined word and the caption. What does each one do for the reader?

check.q: What does a heading do?
choices: Tells what a part of the text is about so a reader can find it
check.why: Headings are signposts. They let a reader jump to the part they need.

check.q: What is a caption?
choices: One sentence that tells what a picture shows
check.why: A caption sits under a picture and explains it in one sentence.

check.q: Which sentence defines a word?
choices: Monarchs migrate, which means they travel far when seasons change.
check.why: Defining means giving the meaning in plain words. The second sentence explains what migrate means.

lessons.title: Writing a How-To
lessons.mainIdea: A how-to lists what you need, then gives numbered steps in the exact order a reader must do them.
reading: Try to make a paper airplane from these directions: "Fold it and throw it." You cannot. A *how-to* is informative writing that teaches a reader to do something, and it only works if the steps are complete and in order. Start with a title that says the job: "How to Make a Paper Airplane That Flies Straight."

Next comes a list of what you need: one sheet of paper, a flat table. Then the *steps*, numbered. Each step is one action, starting with a verb: "1. Fold the paper in half the long way. 2. Open it flat again." Words like first, next, then, after that and finally help the reader keep their place.

The test of a how-to is simple. Give it to someone who has never done the thing, and watch them. Where do they stop and ask? That step is missing something. Where do they do it wrong? That step is unclear. Fix those spots. A how-to is finished when a stranger can follow it without asking you anything.

words.d: writing that teaches a reader to do something step by step
one action in a how-to, done in order

look.title: Find the Missing Step
look.text: How to make a peanut butter sandwich. 1. Get two slices of bread. 2. Spread peanut butter on one slice. 3. Put the slices together. 4. Cut the sandwich in half. A reader stops at step 2 and asks, "With what?" Another reader ends up with the peanut butter on the outside.
look.prompt: What does step 2 leave out? What should step 3 say so the peanut butter ends up inside?

check.q: What comes right after the title in a how-to?
choices: A list of what you need
check.why: The reader needs to gather materials before starting the steps.

check.q: How should each step begin?
check.why: Steps are commands: fold, open, cut. Starting with the verb makes each action clear.

check.q: How do you test a how-to?
choices: Ask a friend if it looks nice
Watch someone who has never done it try to follow it
check.why: Where the stranger stops or goes wrong, the how-to needs a fix.

lessons.title: From Notes to Paragraph
lessons.mainIdea: Writing from research means turning notes in your own words into organized paragraphs, and saying where the facts came from.
reading: Priya wants to write about the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. She reads two books and a museum website. She does not copy sentences. She takes *notes* in her own words, short phrases on index cards: "started Oct 8, 1871." "burned about 3 days." "around 300 people died." "city rebuilt with brick and stone." Each card also says which book or site it came from.

Then she groups the cards, just like sticky notes. One pile: how it started and spread. One pile: what was lost. One pile: how the city rebuilt. Each pile becomes a paragraph. She turns each phrase into a full sentence in her own words. Because the notes were already hers, the paragraphs are hers too.

At the end she lists her *sources*, the places the facts came from. Two reasons. First, it is honest: those writers did the work of finding the facts. Second, a reader who wants more knows where to look. Even a short list, "Books I used," with titles and authors, does the job in fourth grade.

words.d: short phrases in your own words that record facts from a source
the book, website or person a fact came from
finding facts about a topic by reading and asking

look.title: Priya's Note Cards by Pile
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from Priya's imagined cards
look.prompt: Which paragraph will be longest? What should Priya do with the two cards that do not fit?

check.q: How should you take notes from a source?
choices: Short phrases in your own words
check.why: Notes in your own words keep the writing yours and are easy to turn into sentences later.

check.q: Why write down which source each note came from?
choices: So you can list your sources honestly at the end
So you can copy it later
check.why: Naming sources is honest and lets a reader find more.

check.q: What do the grouped piles of cards become?
check.why: Each pile is one group of related facts, and each group becomes a paragraph.

lessons.title: Writing About a Text With Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: When you write about a text, make a point and then prove it with words or details from the text itself.
reading: Suppose the question is "How does the tortoise feel at the start of the race?" You could answer "She feels confident." Good, but a reader might ask how you know. So you add the proof: "When the hare laughs at her, she does not argue. She just says, 'Let us race.'" That proof from the text is *evidence*.

The pattern has three parts. Make your point. Give the evidence, either a short quote in quotation marks or a detail in your own words. Then explain how the evidence proves the point: "Someone who is nervous would argue or back down. She does neither." Point, evidence, explain. Many teachers call it P-E-E.

Choose evidence that really fits. Not every detail proves every point. If your point is that the hare is careless, the fact that he is fast does not help. The fact that he naps in the middle of a race does. Pick the detail that makes your reader nod.

words.d: words or details from a text that prove a point about it
to copy a text's exact words and put them in quotation marks
to tell how the evidence proves the point

look.title: Point, Evidence, Explain
look.text: The hare is careless. In the middle of the race, he lies down under a tree and falls asleep. A runner who cared about winning would never stop to nap with the finish line still ahead.
look.cite: Model answer about the old tortoise-and-hare tale, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which sentence is the point? Which is the evidence? Which one explains?

check.q: What is evidence when you write about a text?
choices: Words or details from the text that prove your point
check.why: Evidence comes from inside the text. It is how you show a reader you are right.

check.q: What are the three parts of the pattern?
check.why: Make the point, give evidence from the text, then explain how the evidence proves it.

check.q: Your point is that the hare is careless. Which detail is the best evidence?
choices: The hare naps in the middle of the race.
The race is on a road.
check.why: Napping mid-race shows carelessness. Being fast does not prove anything about care.

lessons.title: Pacing and Transitions
lessons.mainIdea: Pacing is how fast a piece moves, and transition words carry the reader smoothly from one part to the next.
reading: Theo gave the fort's fall a whole paragraph and the walk home one sentence. That is *pacing*: choosing how much space each part gets. Slow down where the moment matters and speed up where it does not. In informative writing, pacing means giving the important group of facts the most room and the small one the least.

*Transitions* are the words that move a reader between parts. In a story, they handle time: a moment later, by the time we got inside, the next morning. In informative writing, they handle ideas: another reason, in addition, on the other hand, finally. A transition is a hand on the reader's back saying this way.

Read your draft and mark every place the scene, time or idea changes. Is there a transition there? If a reader could get lost, add one. If the transition is doing nothing, cut it. Then check pacing: is the best part the biggest part? If the boring part is longest, cut it down and give the room to the moment that matters.

words.d: how fast a piece of writing moves; how much space each part gets
a word or phrase that moves the reader from one part or idea to the next

look.title: Sentences Per Part in Theo's Second Draft
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the draft described in the story
look.prompt: Where did Theo slow down? Where did he speed up? Why do those choices make sense?

check.q: What is pacing?
choices: How fast a piece moves and how much space each part gets
check.why: Pacing is about space and speed. Slow down where it matters, speed up where it does not.

check.q: Which is a transition that handles time in a story?
check.why: The next morning moves the reader forward in time. The others move between ideas.

check.q: Your draft's longest part is the boring part. What should you do?
choices: Add more to the boring part
Cut it down and give the room to the part that matters
check.why: Good pacing gives the most space to the moment or facts that matter most.

review.q: What is a small moment?
choices: A story about a whole week
One short event a story zooms in on
review.why: A small moment is a few minutes or seconds, told with enough detail that the reader can see it.

review.q: Which opening is the strongest hook?
choices: I am going to tell you about my snow day.
I woke up and got dressed.
review.why: Starting inside the action with a line of talk pulls the reader in.

review.q: Which sentence shows instead of tells?
choices: The hallway was dark and my sneakers squeaked with every step.
review.why: Sensory details, dark and squeaking sneakers, let the reader feel the fear without being told.

review.q: Which ending races to bedtime?
choices: Then we ate dinner and went to sleep. The end.
I did not let go of her all the way home.
The fort was gone, and I did not mind.
review.why: Rushing to the end of the day drains the feeling. A good ending lands on the moment.

review.q: What is the second job of informative writing, after naming the topic?
review.why: Grouping turns a pile of facts into paragraphs a reader can follow.

review.q: What does a caption do?
choices: Tells what a picture shows in one sentence
review.why: A caption sits under a picture and explains what it shows.

review.q: In writing about a text, what comes after the point and the evidence?
choices: An explanation of how the evidence proves the point
review.why: Point, evidence, explain. The explanation connects the proof to the point.

review.q: Which is a transition between ideas in informative writing?
choices: By the time we got inside
review.why: On the other hand moves between ideas. The others move through time in a story.

chapters.title: Revising and Editing
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a rough first draft turn into writing a reader can trust?

story.title: Four Drafts on the Wall
story.kicker: One paragraph about a lost dog. Four versions taped in a row. Watch it get better one draft at a time.
paragraphs: Mr. Nguyen's fifth graders walked into the room and saw four sheets of paper taped in a row across the whiteboard. Each one was a paragraph about the same lost dog, written by Mr. Nguyen himself. "Draft one is on the left," he said. "Draft four is on the right. Find what changed."

Draft one was messy. "my dog got lost and we looked for him and it was bad, we looked evrywhere and then we found him at the park he was ok." Two sentences, one giant run-on, a spelling mistake, no capital at the start. The class groaned. "Everybody's first draft looks like this," Mr. Nguyen said. "Mine too."

Draft two had the same story, but the ideas had moved. He had cut "it was bad" and added what actually happened: the open gate, the empty yard, his sister crying, the two hours of calling. "This is revising," he said. "I changed what it says. I added, I cut, I moved." He had not fixed the spelling yet. "That comes later."

Draft three had strong verbs. "Looked" became "searched." "We went to the park" became "We sprinted to the park." "Dog" became "Biscuit," the dog's real name. Draft four was the editing pass: capitals, periods, a comma in the list of places they searched, quotation marks around what his sister yelled, and "evrywhere" finally spelled right.

Aliyah raised her hand. "Draft four is so much longer." "It is," said Mr. Nguyen. "And draft one was written in ninety seconds. Draft four took me three days. That is the secret nobody tells you. Good writing is mostly rewriting."
story.think: Mr. Nguyen fixed the ideas before he fixed the spelling. Why might that order make sense?

sections.title: A Draft Is Only a Start

lessons.title: Drafting Is Not Finishing
lessons.mainIdea: A first draft is for getting ideas down; the real work of writing happens in the drafts that follow.
reading: Mr. Nguyen's first draft took ninety seconds and looked like a mess. That is normal. A *draft* is a version of a piece of writing, and the first one is only for getting the idea onto the page before it escapes. Nobody expects it to be good. Its only job is to exist.

Many students stop after one draft and hand it in. That is like a builder who nails up the boards and never comes back to paint. The *writing process* has more steps: plan, draft, *revise*, edit, share. Revising and editing are where a rough paragraph becomes one a reader can trust.

Here is the mindset. When you finish a draft, do not ask "Am I done?" Ask "What does this need next?" Sometimes the answer is bigger ideas. Sometimes it is stronger words. Sometimes it is just a missing period. Every draft is a step, and each step has its own job.

words.d: one version of a piece of writing; the first draft is rough on purpose
the steps of writing: plan, draft, revise, edit, share
to change what a piece says: its ideas, order and details

look.title: Ninety Seconds vs Three Days
look.text: Draft one: "my dog got lost and we looked for him and it was bad, we looked evrywhere and then we found him at the park he was ok." Draft four begins: "The gate was open, and the yard was empty. Biscuit was gone."
look.prompt: What can you already tell is different? Why is it not fair to compare a ninety-second draft to a three-day draft?

check.q: What is the only job of a first draft?
choices: To get the idea onto the page
check.why: A first draft exists to capture the idea. Fixing comes in later drafts.

check.q: What are the steps of the writing process?
check.why: Writing is a process with steps. Revising and editing come after the draft.

check.q: What question should you ask when a draft is done?
check.why: Each draft is a step. Asking what it needs next moves the piece forward.

lessons.title: Revising: Add, Cut, Move, Replace
lessons.mainIdea: Revising changes what a piece says, using four moves: add, cut, move and replace.
reading: Look at what happened between draft one and draft two. "It was bad" disappeared. The open gate and the crying sister appeared. The finding at the park moved to the end where it belonged. Those changes are revising: changing the ideas, details and order, not the spelling. Revising happens with a big view of the whole piece.

There are four revising moves. *Add*: put in a detail, a reason or an example the reader needs. *Cut*: take out what is boring, repeated or off topic. Move: put a sentence where it makes more sense, like the best reason last. *Replace*: swap a vague idea for a specific one, like "it was bad" for "my sister cried."

To revise, read the whole draft once without a pencil. Then ask four questions. What is missing? What is not needed? What is in the wrong place? What is vague? Each question matches one move. Mark the spot, make the change, and read the whole thing again. One good revising pass beats ten drafts of fiddling.

words.d: to put in a detail or idea the reader needs
to take out what is boring, repeated or off topic
to put a sentence or idea where it makes more sense
to swap a weak or vague word or idea for a stronger, more specific one

look.title: Revising Moves From Draft One to Draft Two
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from Mr. Nguyen's drafts described in the story
look.prompt: Which move did he use most? Why does a thin first draft usually need a lot of adding?

check.q: Which of these is revising, not editing?
choices: Cutting a sentence that repeats an idea
check.why: Revising changes what the piece says. Cutting a repeated idea is a revising move.

check.q: Swapping "it was bad" for "my sister cried" is which move?
check.why: Replace swaps a vague idea for a specific one.

check.q: What should you do before you start marking changes?
check.why: Revising needs a big view. Read it all first, then ask what is missing, extra, misplaced or vague.

lessons.title: Feedback That Helps
lessons.mainIdea: Good feedback from a reader is specific, kind and about the writing, and it always includes a question.
reading: "It's good." "I liked it." Those are nice to hear, but they do not help a writer revise. Useful *feedback* is specific. "I could really see the empty yard" tells the writer what is working. "I got confused about where you were when you found him" tells the writer what to fix. A *peer*, a classmate reading your work, can give both.

A simple shape for feedback. First, say one thing that worked and point to the exact sentence. Second, ask one honest question: "How long did you look?" or "What did your sister say?" A question is better than a command, because the writer gets to decide how to answer it on the page.

Two rules for the writer. Listen without arguing. If a reader was confused, they were confused; explaining it out loud does not fix the page. And you do not have to take every suggestion. Feedback tells you where a reader stumbled. You decide how to fix it. It is still your writing.

words.d: what a reader tells a writer about how the writing worked for them
a classmate or someone your own age
exact; pointing to one sentence or moment rather than the whole piece

look.title: Two Readers
look.text: Maya reads Jonah's story. Reader one says, "It's good, I liked the dog." Reader two says, "The part where the gate was open gave me chills. But I lost track of the time. How long were you looking before you thought of the park?"
look.prompt: Which feedback can Jonah actually use? What would he add to his draft?

check.q: Why is "It's good" weak feedback?
choices: It does not point to anything the writer can use
check.why: Useful feedback is specific. It names what worked and where a reader stumbled.

check.q: Why is a question better than a command in feedback?
choices: The writer decides how to answer it on the page
check.why: A question shows where the reader wanted more and leaves the choice with the writer.

check.q: A reader says they were confused. What should the writer do?
choices: Explain it out loud until they understand
check.why: Explaining out loud does not fix the writing. Listen and then decide how to fix the confusing spot.

lessons.title: Strong Verbs and Exact Nouns
lessons.mainIdea: A strong verb and an exact noun do more work than a weak word propped up with extra ones.
reading: "We went to the park really fast." Now: "We sprinted to the park." The second one is shorter and you can see it. Went is a weak *verb*; it could mean anything. Sprinted is a strong verb; it tells you exactly how. Strong verbs let you cut props like really and very, because the verb already carries the picture.

The same goes for *nouns*, the words for people, places and things. "The dog" could be any dog. "Biscuit" is one dog. "A bird" could be anything with feathers. "A cardinal" is red and you can see it. An exact noun makes a picture without needing a pile of describing words in front of it.

Try this on your draft. Circle every went, got, said, did, thing and stuff. For each one, ask: what exactly? Went how? Got what? Said in what voice? Replace what you can. Do not replace all of them; "said" is fine most of the time. But one sprinted where you had went can wake up a whole paragraph.

words.d: an action word; a strong verb shows exactly how the action happens
a word for a person, place or thing; an exact noun names one specific thing

look.title: A Line That Sees Exactly
look.text: Dark brown is the river, / Golden is the sand.
look.cite: Robert Louis Stevenson, "Where Go the Boats?", A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885
look.prompt: The poet could have written "The river is a color." What do the exact words dark brown and golden let you see?

check.q: Why is sprinted stronger than went really fast?
choices: The verb itself shows how, so no props are needed
check.why: A strong verb carries the picture. Really and very become unnecessary.

check.q: Which is the most exact noun?
check.why: Cardinal names one kind of bird and makes a picture. Thing, animal and bird get less exact.

check.q: Should you replace every said in your draft?
choices: No; said is fine most of the time
check.why: Replace weak words where it helps. Said is plain and usually best; changing every one sounds forced.

lessons.title: Sentence Variety
lessons.mainIdea: Mixing short and long sentences, and different openings, keeps a reader awake.
reading: Read this out loud. "I saw the gate. It was open. The yard was empty. Biscuit was gone. I ran inside. I yelled for my mom." Every sentence is short. Every one starts with I. It sounds like a drum with one beat. Now: "When I saw the open gate and the empty yard, my stomach dropped. Biscuit was gone." Long, then short. The short one hits harder because of the long one before it.

That is *sentence variety*: mixing sentence lengths and sentence starts. Short sentences are for punch. Long sentences are for building up or slowing down. Starts can be a name, a time word, an action or a place: "That night," "Under the porch," "Screaming his name," "Biscuit."

Two easy fixes. If you have three short sentences in a row, *combine* two with and, but, when or because. If every sentence starts the same way, move a phrase to the front of one of them. Then read it aloud again. You will hear the rhythm change.

words.d: mixing short and long sentences and different sentence openings
to join two short sentences into one with a word like and, but, when or because

look.title: Words per Sentence in Two Versions
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the two versions in the reading
look.prompt: Version A is all short. Version B is long, then short. Which one would you rather read aloud, and why?

check.q: What is sentence variety?
check.why: Variety means a mix. Short for punch, long for build-up, with different starts.

check.q: Why does "Biscuit was gone" hit harder after a long sentence?
choices: Because it has a name in it
Because the contrast with the long sentence makes the short one stand out
Because it is the last sentence
check.why: A short sentence after a long one lands with force because of the contrast.

check.q: You have three short sentences in a row. What is one fix?
choices: Add the word very to each one
Combine two with and, but, when or because
check.why: Combining two of them creates a longer sentence and breaks the drumbeat.

lessons.title: Capitals and Commas in a Series
lessons.mainIdea: Editing fixes the rules: capitals at sentence starts and on names, and commas between items in a list.
reading: Revising is done. Now comes *editing*: fixing the mechanics so the reader is never distracted. Start with *capital* letters. Every sentence begins with one. Every name of a person, a pet, a city, a street, a day or a month gets one: Biscuit, Chicago, Tuesday, March. The word I is always a capital, even in the middle.

Now the *series* comma. A series is a list of three or more things in a sentence. "We searched the yard the alley the park and the school." Read that out loud; the places run together. Put a comma between each item: "We searched the yard, the alley, the park, and the school." The comma before and is called the serial comma. Many schools teach it; some newspapers skip it. Either way, be consistent.

Edit with a pencil, one rule at a time. First pass: capitals only. Second pass: commas in lists only. Trying to catch everything at once means missing half of it. Slow, single-rule passes catch what a fast read never sees.

words.d: to fix capitals, punctuation, spelling and grammar so the writing is correct
an uppercase letter, used at the start of a sentence and on names
a list of three or more items in a sentence, separated by commas

look.title: Edit This Sentence
look.text: Here is a sentence from a draft: "on saturday my cousin luis and i took the train to chicago and ate tacos popcorn and ice cream." It has five missing capitals and two missing commas.
look.prompt: Find every word that needs a capital. Where do the two commas go?

check.q: Which words always get a capital letter?
choices: Names of people, places, days and months, and the word I
Only the first word of a paragraph
check.why: Sentence starts, names of specific people, places, days and months, and I are capitalized.

check.q: What is a series?
choices: A list of three or more items in a sentence
check.why: A series is a list of three or more things, and commas separate the items.

check.q: Why edit one rule at a time?
choices: Because editing is faster that way
Because you catch more when you look for one thing
Because there is only one rule
check.why: A single-rule pass catches errors a fast read-through misses.

lessons.title: Quotation Marks in Dialogue
lessons.mainIdea: Quotation marks go around the exact words a person says, with a comma or end mark inside them.
reading: Mr. Nguyen's sister yelled something in the yard. On the page it looks like this: "Biscuit!" she yelled. "Where are you?" The marks around her words are *quotation marks*. They tell the reader: these are the exact words that came out of her mouth. Words outside the marks, like she yelled, are the writer's.

Three rules make dialogue clean. First, the quotation marks wrap only the spoken words. Second, the punctuation at the end of the spoken words goes inside the closing mark: "I'm okay," he said. Notice the comma, not a period, when the sentence keeps going with he said. Third, a new speaker gets a new line. When the sister stops and Mom starts, start a new paragraph.

The *speech tag* is the part like she yelled or he said. It can come before or after the words. "We'll find him," Mom said. Or: Mom said, "We'll find him." Either way there is a comma between the tag and the words. If a question mark or exclamation point ends the speech, it replaces the comma: "Where?" she asked.

words.d: the marks that go around a speaker's exact words
the words that tell who is speaking, like she said or he yelled
the words characters say to each other

look.title: Two Speakers, Two Lines
look.text: "He's not under the porch," my sister said. Her voice was shaking. "Then we go to the park," Mom said, and she was already grabbing her keys.
look.cite: Model dialogue written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find each speech tag. Where is the punctuation for each spoken sentence, inside or outside the marks?

check.q: What goes inside quotation marks?
choices: The exact words a person says
check.why: Quotation marks wrap only the spoken words. The tag stays outside.

check.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
check.why: The comma goes inside the closing mark, and the tag follows in lowercase.

check.q: What do you do when a new person starts talking?
check.why: A new speaker gets a new line. It keeps the reader from mixing up who said what.

lessons.title: Apostrophes
lessons.mainIdea: An apostrophe shows a missing letter in a contraction or shows that something belongs to someone.
reading: Look at the small mark in don't and in Biscuit's. It is an *apostrophe*, and it does two different jobs. In don't, it stands in for a missing letter: do not squeezed into one word, with the o gone. Words like that are *contractions*: can't, I'm, she's, we'll, isn't. The apostrophe goes exactly where the missing letters were.

In Biscuit's collar, the apostrophe shows that the collar belongs to Biscuit. That is a *possessive*. Add an apostrophe and s to a name or a singular noun: my sister's voice, the dog's bowl. For a plural noun that already ends in s, put the apostrophe after the s: the dogs' bowls means bowls for more than one dog.

The trap: its and it's. It's always means it is or it has: "It's cold." Its, with no apostrophe, means belonging to it: "The dog wagged its tail." Test it by saying it is out loud. "The dog wagged it is tail" is wrong, so no apostrophe. And plain plurals never get one: two dogs, three parks, no apostrophe at all.

words.d: the mark that shows missing letters in a contraction or shows belonging
two words squeezed into one, like don't or I'm
a word form that shows something belongs to someone, like Biscuit's

look.title: Which Job Is It Doing?
look.text: Read these four: 1. We couldn't find him. 2. My sister's flashlight died. 3. It's almost dark. 4. The park closes its gates at nine. One of them has no apostrophe on purpose.
look.prompt: For each apostrophe, is it standing in for missing letters or showing belonging? Why does number 4 have no apostrophe?

check.q: In don't, what does the apostrophe show?
check.why: Don't is a contraction of do not. The apostrophe marks where the o was.

check.q: Which is correct?
check.why: Its means belonging to it. It's means it is, which would not make sense here.

check.q: How do you write the bowls that belong to several dogs?
check.why: For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe goes after the s.

lessons.title: Spelling Strategies
lessons.mainIdea: Good spellers use strategies: word parts, patterns, a personal word list and a dictionary check.
reading: "Evrywhere" sat in Mr. Nguyen's draft for three versions. He was not a bad speller; he was a fast drafter, and that is fine. Spelling gets fixed in editing. But you need strategies, ways to catch and fix words, because you will not always have a computer to underline them in red.

Strategy one: break the word into parts. Every-where. Un-believe-able. If you can spell the parts, you can spell the word. Strategy two: know the patterns. When a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before adding ing: hope, hoping. For words that end in y after a consonant, change y to i before adding es or ed: cry, cried. Patterns cover thousands of words.

Strategy three: keep a *personal word list*, the five or ten words you get wrong again and again. Check your draft against it every time. Strategy four: when you are not sure, circle the word and keep writing. Look it up in a dictionary or ask at the end. Never let one hard word stop the whole draft.

words.d: a plan or method for solving a problem, like breaking a word into parts
a spelling rule that works for many words, like dropping a silent e before ing
your own short list of words you often misspell

look.title: Words Fixed by Each Strategy in One Class Draft
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from a sample class editing pass
look.prompt: Which strategy fixed the most words? Why might knowing patterns pay off more than any other strategy?

check.q: How does breaking a word into parts help spelling?
choices: If you can spell the parts, you can spell the word
check.why: Every-where and un-believe-able are easier as parts than as one long word.

check.q: What happens to hope when you add ing?
check.why: Drop the silent e before adding ing. Hope becomes hoping.

check.q: You are drafting and hit a word you cannot spell. What should you do?
choices: Stop writing until you find it
Leave the word out of the story
Circle it, keep writing, and check it later
check.why: Spelling gets fixed in editing. One hard word should never stop the draft.

lessons.title: Read It Aloud
lessons.mainIdea: Reading your draft out loud lets your ears catch mistakes your eyes skip over.
reading: Your eyes cheat. They know what you meant to write, so they read the missing word as if it were there. Your ears do not cheat. Read this out loud: "We searched the yard the alley the park." You will run out of breath and hear the missing commas. Read a run-on aloud and you will hear where the period was supposed to be.

Reading *aloud* catches four things. Missing or doubled words. Sentences that go on too long. Sentences that all sound the same. And places where the meaning is unclear, because you will stumble there. When you stumble, mark it. Do not fix it yet. Finish the read, then go back to every mark.

Do it slowly, with your finger on the words, so you read what is on the page, not what is in your head. Better yet, have a partner read your draft aloud to you. They do not know what you meant, so they read exactly what is there. Where they stumble is where your reader will stumble.

words.d: out loud, so you can hear it
two or more sentences jammed together without the right punctuation

look.title: Your Ears Will Catch It
look.text: Read this draft sentence out loud, slowly: "We looked for for Biscuit for two hours and my sister was crying and then Mom said the park and we ran and there he was by the swings eating a hot dog someone dropped."
look.prompt: What did your ears catch that your eyes might have skipped? Where would you put a period?

check.q: Why do your eyes miss mistakes in your own draft?
choices: Because the print is too small
Because they know what you meant and read it that way
check.why: Your brain fills in what you meant. Your ears hear what is really there.

check.q: What should you do when you stumble while reading aloud?
choices: Stop and rewrite the whole draft
Mark it and keep going, then fix all marks after
check.why: Mark the stumbles, finish the read, then go back. Stopping each time breaks the flow.

check.q: Why is a partner a good reader for your draft?
choices: Partners do not need to mark anything
They read what is on the page, not what you meant
check.why: A partner does not know your intentions, so their stumbles show real problems.

lessons.title: Type It and Share It
lessons.mainIdea: Typing a final copy and sharing it with a real reader is the last step of the process, and it is the reason for all the rest.
reading: When the revising and editing are done, make a clean copy. Most classes type it. Typing has real benefits: the spelling checker underlines words to look at, you can move a sentence without erasing, and a reader can read it easily. But the checker is not your editor. It misses there for their and it's for its. Your own editing passes still come first.

A *final copy* needs a title, your name and the date. Use one plain font, and put a space between paragraphs or indent the first line. Print it or save it with a clear file name, like snow-day-story-final. Keep your earlier drafts too. They show how far the piece came, and sometimes a cut sentence turns out to be worth putting back.

Then *share* it. Read it to the class, post it on the wall, put it in a class book, or send it to the person it was for. Writing is a message, and a message that never reaches a reader is not finished. Mr. Nguyen's four drafts stayed on the wall all year, so every student could remember what a first draft looks like and what it can become.

words.d: the clean, finished version of a piece, ready for a reader
to give your finished writing to a real reader or audience
a computer tool that underlines words it does not recognize

look.title: A Word Comes Alive When It Is Shared
look.text: A word is dead / When it is said, / Some say. / I say it just / Begins to live / That day.
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, short poem published after her death in 1894
look.prompt: Dickinson says a word begins to live when it is said. How is sharing your writing like saying a word out loud?

check.q: What can a spelling checker miss?
choices: Real words used in the wrong place, like there for their
check.why: The checker only knows if a word exists, not if it is the right word. Your own editing catches those.

check.q: Why keep your earlier drafts?
choices: They show how far the piece came, and a cut line might be worth restoring
The teacher collects them for points
Final copies are not allowed without them
check.why: Drafts are a record of the work and sometimes hold a sentence you want back.

check.q: Why is sharing part of the writing process?
choices: Because typing takes a long time
Because writing is a message, and a message needs a reader
Because it is the easiest step
check.why: Writing exists to reach a reader. Until it is shared, the message is not delivered.

review.q: What is the difference between revising and editing?
choices: Revising fixes spelling; editing changes ideas
Revising changes ideas and order; editing fixes mechanics
review.why: Revising changes what a piece says. Editing fixes capitals, punctuation and spelling afterward.

review.q: Which is a revising move?
review.why: Cutting is one of the four revising moves: add, cut, move, replace.

review.q: Which feedback is most useful?
choices: I lost track of where you were when you found him. How far was the park?
review.why: Specific feedback names a spot and asks a question the writer can answer on the page.

review.q: Which sentence uses a strong verb?
choices: We went to the park quickly.
We really went to the park.
We went very fast to the park.
review.why: Sprinted shows exactly how, so the props really and very are not needed.

review.q: Which sentence has the comma placed correctly?
review.why: In dialogue, the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, and the tag follows.

review.q: Which is correct?
review.why: Its shows belonging. It's would mean it is, which does not fit.

review.q: What is the best way to spell hoping from hope?
review.why: Drop the silent e before adding ing.

review.q: Why read your draft aloud?
choices: Your ears catch mistakes your eyes skip
review.why: Eyes read what you meant; ears hear what is really on the page.
